articles.text: Voter’s Edge nonpartisan guide ready in time for Nov. 3 election The League of Women Voters of California has produced a comprehensive, nonpartisan online guide to elections, covering federal, state, and local races. The online document, called Voter’s Edge, aims to provide all Californians with reliable voter resources to counter the surge of misinformation in the news. The League describes Voter’s Edge as the “Gold Standard in voter information”, and the only one that offers campaign finance data. It also helps you find your polling location or where to drop off your ballot. This past week, the website garnered over 4 million views. The League of Women Voters of California Education Fund produced one of the nation’s first election information websites, SmartVoter.org. Since 1996, the Smart Voter project has been California’s premier online source for authoritative, nonpartisan coverage of election contests, candidates, and ballot measures. MapLight’s Voter’s Edge tool was first designed to help voters understand the sources of funding behind ballot measures in California. In some years, the project has also covered candidates and elections in states beyond California. In 2014, the League and MapLight joined forces to create a successful pilot project. articles.text: The headline in the East Bay Times read; “Relax, Oakland… Gerald the turkey has been captured.” It was big news. Gerald, a wild turkey had taken up residence in Oakland’s Morcom Rose Garden and because of his aggressive, bullying behavior toward garden visitors, had forced its closure. Agencies like the Oakland Parks Department, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and Oakland Animal Services debated what to do. Some thought he should be trapped, although he proved adept at avoiding capture. Some thought he should be killed, although that seemed a punishment more extreme than the crime. Finally, in late October, Rebecca Dmytryk, director of Wildlife Emergency Services, got Gerald’s attention with some of his favorite food, sunflower seeds and blueberries, and pretended to be an older woman. Predictably, Gerald, notorious for his aggressive behavior toward those he perceived to be weak and fearful, came closer. Dmytryk grabbed him by the scruff of the neck and wrapped her arms around him. With the assistance of her husband they got him into a large carrier. Fish and Wildlife officials then came and took Gerald to the hills of Orinda where wild turkeys thrive, tagged him and released him. Dmytrk said the whole episode could have been avoided if human beings would have refrained from feeding wildlife, in this case Gerald. That is a good lesson. Perhaps there is another lesson. For those of us who spend our time in religious communities like churches, the behaviors exhibited by Gerald – aggressive, bullying, demanding, targeting those perceived to be weak – are far from unfamiliar. Let’s commit to stop rewarding Geraldish behavior. If you act like Gerald, you don’t get attention. If you act like Gerald, you don’t get to be chair of the committee. If you act like Gerald, you don’t get to share your opinion. If you act like Gerald, you don’t deserve to be the pastor. Perhaps there is still one more

articles.text: The following article was originally sent prior to the November The upcoming Piedmont elections will have important measures and candidates on the ballot that will lead Piedmont to becoming more environmentally conscious. Learn what your vote means for Piedmont, the difference it will make in the years to come, and what your City Council Candidates have to say about it. Measure UU – the Pool Bond The objective is to prevent permanent closure of the Piedmont community pool. Our current pool is 56 years old and is far overdue for some fixing up. Conna McCarthy notes, “We either have to rebuild it, or we have to close it.” Moreover, the current state of the pool is unsustainable for the environment. Council member Jen Cavenaugh says the community pool leaks more than 3,000 gallons of water a day, or over 1 million gallons Since there is only one pool in Piedmont, it is often used by many. Parents bring their kids to learn how to swim, high school teams practice sports, and it is even used for rehabilitating injuries. According to council candidate Connie Herrick, a longtime Piedmont Pool member, “It is really important that we pass [measure UU] next month; each time we delay, we push out several years. At this point, in the best-case scenario, we’re going to be open maybe in 2024, so we really can’t delay anymore.” Measure TT – The Transfer Tax The transfer tax funds can be used for various purposes which is why voting for environmentally friendly council members is crucial. They can help ensure the general fund is used for more environmentally concious decision-making. For example, ecofriendly equipment replacement, solar energy options, and sustainable landscaping. Opponents argue that when Measure TT was written, there were no safeguards that ensure the money will be spent the way voters would like. In this case, money from transfer taxes can be used for any means such as salaries, pensions, project over-runs, etc. Voting for candidates that are sure of using funds for pressing issues and eco-friendly spending is key. How are our City Council candidates adressing climate action? Jen Cavenaugh, a City Council member completing her first four-year term, has a history of community service related to the environment. Cavenaugh is a member of Piedmont Connect, an organization that supports city efforts to become a more sustainable city. She is also involved with The Imperfect Food customer buying program, which ships imperfect products with eco-friendly packaging, minimizing waste. “No plastic, no extra packaging,” Cavenaugh says. On the environmental quality committee, she advocated for a bill focused on product consumption and making sure residents “push the burden on the manufacturers. When you do that, suddenly they are accountable, and now they have an incentive to do better.” Connie Herrick is participating in the Piedmont Climate Challenge, which prompts its participants to reduce food waste, eat less meat, shop local, recycle, turn off lights, and change their means of transportation to be more environmentally friendly. She supports the current Climate Action Plan and is in favor of implementing a climate committee. “We need a climate action committee. As you know, our city has all these committees. We’ve got public safety, recreation, parks, we even have one for the pedestrian bikeway. But we don’t have one for climate action. And if it’s that important to us, which it is, then we need to have that commitment.” Conna McCarthy fully supports Piedmont doing its part to protect the earth’s climate. Working off the climate action plan, she speaks fondly of the reach proposal. “We are asking people to go beyond to help mitigate climate change by lowering their carbon footprint,” she said. The proposal leans towards becoming more dependant on electric, renewable energy. “There’s a menu with about seven energy efficient items. When someone does a construction project over a certain value, it triggers that homeowner to choose from the menu,” she said. The reach will allow our city to make the switch from unsustainable items that contribute to greenhouse gas emissions, to more eco-friendly options. My takeaway Piedmont has many environmentally friendly candidates, giving voters multiple options for how they want the city to be run. This election is about more than whether or not our candidates are environmentally friendly, it’s about how they are environmentally friendly. And no time is better than the present to take part in determining the future of our city. Ed. Note: Emily Ballati and her family have recently moved to Piedmont from Oakland. She is a junior at Bishop O’Dowd High School.

pages.text: Wednesday, November 4, 2020 3 News Things are heating up – an environmental election By Emily Ballati The following article was originally sent prior to the November 3 election. The upcoming Piedmont elections will have important measures and candidates on the ballot that will lead Piedmont to becoming more environmentally conscious. Learn what your vote means for Piedmont, the difference it will make in the years to come, and what your City Council Candidates have to say about it. Measure UU – the Pool Bond The objective is to prevent permanent closure of the Piedmont community pool. Our current pool is 56 years old and is far overdue for some fixing up. Conna McCarthy notes, “We either have to rebuild it, or we have to close it.” Moreover, the current state of the pool is unsustainable for the environment. Council member Jen Cavenaugh says the community pool leaks more than 3,000 gallons of water a day, or over 1 million gallons per year. Since there is only one pool in Piedmont, it is often used by many. Parents bring their kids to learn how to swim, high school teams practice sports, and it is even used for rehabilitating injuries. According to council candidate Connie Herrick, a longtime Piedmont Pool member, “It is really important that we pass [measure UU] next month; each time we delay, we push out several years. At this point, in the best-case scenario, we’re going to be open maybe in 2024, so we really can’t delay anymore.” Measure TT – The Transfer Tax The transfer tax funds can be used for various purposes which is why voting for environmentally friendly council members is crucial. They can help ensure the general fund is used for more environmentally concious decision-making. For example, ecofriendly equipment replacement, solar energy options, and sustainable landscaping. Opponents argue that when Measure TT was written, there were no safeguards that ensure the money will be spent the way voters would like. In this case, money from transfer taxes can be used for any means such as salaries, pensions, project over-runs, etc. Voting for candidates that are sure of using funds for pressing issues and eco-friendly spending is key. How are our City Council candidates adressing climate action? Jen Cavenaugh, a City Council member completing her first four-year term, has a history of community service related to the environment. Cavenaugh is a member of Piedmont Connect, an organization that supports city efforts to become a more sustainable city. She is also involved with The Imperfect Food customer buying program, which ships imperfect products with eco-friendly packaging, minimizing waste. “No plastic, no extra packaging,” Cavenaugh says. On the environmental quality committee, she advocated for a bill focused on product consumption and making sure residents “push the burden on the manufacturers. When you do that, suddenly they are accountable, and now they have an incentive to do better.” Connie Herrick is participating in the Piedmont Climate Challenge, which prompts its participants to reduce food waste, eat less meat, shop local, recycle, turn off lights, and change their means of transportation to be more environmentally friendly. She supports the current Climate Action Plan and is in favor of implementing a climate committee. “We need a climate action committee. As you know, our city has all these committees. We’ve got public safety, recreation, parks, we even have one for the pedestrian bikeway. But we don’t have one for climate action. And if it’s that important to us, which it is, then we need to have that commitment.” Conna McCarthy fully supports Piedmont doing its part to protect the earth’s climate. Working off the climate action plan, she speaks fondly of the reach proposal. “We are asking people to go beyond to help mitigate climate change by lowering their carbon footprint,” she said. The proposal leans towards becoming more dependant on electric, renewable energy. “There’s a menu with about seven energy efficient items. When someone does a construction project over a certain value, it triggers that homeowner to choose from the menu,” she said. The reach will allow our city to make the switch from unsustainable items that contribute to greenhouse gas emissions, to more eco-friendly options. My takeaway Piedmont has many environmentally friendly candidates, giving voters multiple options for how they want the city to be run. This election is about more than whether or not our candidates are environmentally friendly, it’s about how they are environmentally friendly. And no time is better than the present to take part in determining the future of our city. Ed. Note: Emily Ballati and her family have recently moved to Piedmont from Oakland. She is a junior at Bishop O’Dowd High School. articles.text: Wildfire season continues; August Complex Fire burns over 1 million acres October was markedly warm and dry in the Bay Area, the National Weather Service said November 1, although cooler weather is expected to move into the region this weekend. Across the Bay Area and Central Coast, average temperatures during October 2020 were 4 to 7 degrees hotter than normal. Additionally, most areas received no rain for the entire month. After hot, gusty conditions blew across the region last week, officials were concerned that more wildfires would break out and a Red Flag Warning was issued for the entire Bay Area. Although Cal Fire responded to several fires in Northern California the past week, the new blazes were quickly contained. The Red Flag Warning expired on Tuesday, October 27. “A big pattern change is still being forecast on Friday and over the weekend,” NWS Bay Area said this week, adding that the region might see scattered showers this weekend. “We are moving into a typical fall weather pattern, with cool and moist evenings,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black. “The biggest wildfire threat for the fall occurs when we see wind and humidity interplay creating significant potential for wildfire.” Black noted that wildfire risk will only be reduced with heavy and consistent rain. “Until we see significant and sustained rain, we will continue to see exceptionally low fuel moistures and high ‘Probability of Ignition,’” he added. Air quality in Piedmont has remained moderate or better for the past few days, and this outlook is expected to continue. Some smokey haze drifted over the area last weekend due to fires that are burning along the Sierra Nevada mountain range to the east. Both Cal Fire and Black noted that “wildfire season” will last through November. Some of the most devastating wildfires in California history, such as the 2018 Camp Fire, began in November. “The Camp Fire started on November 8 in conditions similar to our current weather,” Black continued. “Piedmont residents traveling for Thanksgiving are reminded to stay vigilant and informed for wildfire threats.” Five of the top 20 largest wildfires in state history have occurred this year. The August Complex Fire, which continues to burn in and around Mendocino National Forest, is the largest wildfire in California history and is the first fire to burn over 1 million acres in the state. The fire, which was caused by lightning back in August, is now 91 percent contained. The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. Black recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org.

articles.text: Council shifts $500,000 from General fund to facilities maintenance City finances are in good shape, despite negative fiscal impacts related to COVID-19. Such was the message from the Piedmont City Council as it reviewed year-end fund transfers, appropriations, and adjustments at an October 19 meeting. The Council unanimously approved a year-end transfer of $500,000 from the general fund to the facilities maintenance fund. In fiscal year 2019-20 (July 1, 2019 to June 30, 2020), favorable revenue trends and lower than anticipated expenses resulted in a net income of approximately $804,000 in the general fund. The city’s general funds can be used for any discretionary spending and finances many of the basic municipal services such as public safety or public works. The transfer of $500,000 to the city’s facilities maintenance fund would result in a General Fund ending balance of $5.6 million, representing 21 percent of operating expenditures, consistent with prior years. The council took similar action in October 2019 to distribute excess net revenue. Facilities maintenance funds go toward any and all city facilities, except for the community pool. This includes annual repairs for each facility (including parks and walkways), scheduled maintenance, and capital projects. All operating city department expenditures were lower than budgeted except for the Public Works Department, according to the staff report authored by City Finance Director Michael Szczech. Public Works expenses exceeded budget due to overages in city engineering, tree pruning, janitorial (due to COVID-19), and utilities expense. These costs were partially offset by savings in personnel and equipment related costs. The Finance Department recommended that the FY 2019-20 appropriation be increased by $56,574, which was approved by city council. Non-Departmental expenses exceeded budget due to higher than expected workers compensation claims. Workers compensation costs exceeded budget by $23,254. The city anticipated a financial fallout due to COVID-19, as evidenced by a June 1 meeting earlier this year. At that meeting, property transfer taxes, business and sales taxes and recreational revenues were all projected to be down. Szczech wrote in a June 1 staff report that the city budget would be balanced by adjustments to deferred maintenance and facilities maintenance, and that improvements to city facilities, such as the community pool and City Hall upgrades, will be on hold. Measure UU, a $19.5 million bond to rebuild the community pool, is the only current plan to repair the aging facility. No funds from the general fund nor the facilities maintenance fund will be used to repair the pool. Property tax revenue will not be affected for fiscal year 2020- 21, City Administrator Sara Lillevand said in her June 1 report to the council. That revenue is budgeted at $15,135,000, an increase of $540,000 from 2019-20.
articles.title: City Finances in good shape despite COVID-19 impact

articles.text: One of the most important tenets of the Scout Law is “a Scout is helpful”. For 36 years the Piedmont Scouts BSA has collected food and funds to help feed families in Alameda County. Last year Piedmont residents were especially generous, donating 8,095 pounds of food and $6,215 in cash to the Food Bank. This year’s event is moving to online donations, and the Scouts have set an ambitious goal of raising $7,500. Instead of a one-day annual food collection drive, this year’s campaign will last for five weeks, from November 1 through December 6. In addition, every Tuesday is Giving Back Tuesday. “We hope that those who have so generously donated food in the past will give online this year to help us combat food insecurity,” said Katy Kobal, Scouting for Food Chair. Every dollar donated allows the Food Bank to purchase $7 worth of food. We estimate that our need has doubled in Alameda county,” said Suzan Bateson, Executive Director of the Alameda County Community Food Bank. “October was our biggest month in food distribution ever. We anticipated distributing five million pounds of food. That is record-breaking, stunning.” Pre-COVID, Alameda County had one of the highest incidences of hunger in the nation. One in five residents of the county live below the poverty line. Of those Piedmont Troop 6 Scouts John Cumbelich (left) and Jack GrossWhitaker present a check in the amount of $3395.90 for the Alameda County Food Bank to newscasters from KPIX in November 2018 at the conclusion of the annual Scouting for Food campaign. receiving assistance from the Alameda County Food Bank, two-thirds are children and the elderly. How the food bank helps Yvonne and her family are just one example of the many families that are struggling during this pandemic. Yvonne is a mom who enjoys spending time with her two children: 11-year-old Elliott and 10-year-old Jordan. She owns a day care facility but had to close it at the beginning of March due to the pandemic. Her husband still works at an insurance company; however, scaling down to one income has been challenging. “Things are a lot tighter. While things are different and money is tight, Yvonne said she’s thankful she’s able to spend more time with her children. articles.text: More than half of the world’s population is bilingual, and the number of bilingual speakers in the U.S. is growing. So too is the body of research looking at the effects of bilingualism, which shows many cognitive advantages compared to monolingualism. Those include increased vocabulary, listening and reading skills, advanced problem solving, flexible thinking, and multi-tasking. In some cases, the bilingualism is forced, such as when a family moves to a country with a different language. In other instances, the bilingualism is optional, such as when a family decides to enroll their child in an immersion program in preschool or kindergarten. Simultaneous bilinguals learn two languages from birth, while sequential bilinguals learn a first language, and later introduce a second. Regardless of the specific circumstance, children have an enormous capacity for developing more than one language. With regard to supporting bilingual learners, the goal is simple: provide a high quantity of high-quality exposure to each language. The exact manner in which to accomplish this seems to be causing some confusion and conflicting advice to parents. For example, some parents are advised to take a structured approach based on a person, with one parent speaking one language and the other parent speaking the other. (In this situation, preference should be given to the language proficiency of each family member.) Some parents are advised to take a structured approach based on place, with one language spoken in the home and the other at school. And other families find a flexible use of both languages, without fixed rules, leads to balanced exposure and positive results. Some of the developmental guidelines for bilingual children also seem to be causing some confusion. Most bilingual children speak their first words by the time they are 1 year old, as is the case for monolingual children. Most bilingual children combine words into short phrases by the time they are 2 years old, as is the case with monolingual children. These early vocabulary words can be in one or both languages. As language develops, bilingual children may mix grammar rules, and/or use words from both languages within the same sentence. This is an entirely normal part of becoming a bilingual speaker. Some bilingual children, particularly sequential bilinguals, may not talk very much when they begin using their second language. This silent period may last several weeks or months and is also a normal part of becoming a bilingual speaker. I have regular conversations with parents regarding children who are exposed to multiple language, and are thinking that their children are “confused” or “delayed” due to multiple language exposure, or bilingualism. Bilingual children are not more likely than monolingual children to have difficulties with language, show delays in learning, or be diagnosed with a language disorder. But parent perceptions are often otherwise, revealing a disconnect from scientific findings. If a bilingual child is exhibiting symptoms of a speech, language and/or reading delay or difficulty, it will be evident in both languages, and should be evaluated by a professional. And if the child is not, parents should continue to provide a high quantity of high-quality exposure to each language. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. For 36 years the Piedmont Scouts BSA has collected food and funds to help feed families in Alameda County. Last year Piedmont residents were especially generous, donating 8,095 pounds of food and $6,215 in cash to the Food Bank. This year’s event is moving to online donations, and the Scouts have set an ambitious goal of raising $7,500. Instead of a one-day annual food collection drive, this year’s campaign will last for five weeks, from November 1 through December 6. In addition, every Tuesday is Giving Back Tuesday. “We hope that those who have so generously donated food in the past will give online this year to help us combat food insecurity,” said Katy Kobal, Scouting for Food Chair. Every dollar donated allows the Food Bank to purchase $7 worth of food. We estimate that our need has doubled in Alameda county,” said Suzan Bateson, Executive Director of the Alameda County Community Food Bank. “October was our biggest month in food distribution ever. We anticipated distributing five million pounds of food. That is record-breaking, stunning.” Pre-COVID, Alameda County had one of the highest incidences of hunger in the nation. One in five residents of the county live below the poverty line. Of those Piedmont Troop 6 Scouts John Cumbelich (left) and Jack GrossWhitaker present a check in the amount of $3395.90 for the Alameda County Food Bank to newscasters from KPIX in November 2018 at the conclusion of the annual Scouting for Food campaign. receiving assistance from the Alameda County Food Bank, two-thirds are children and the elderly. How the food bank helps Yvonne and her family are just one example of the many families that are struggling during this pandemic. Yvonne is a mom who enjoys spending time with her two children: 11-year-old Elliott and 10-year-old Jordan. She owns a day care facility but had to close it at the beginning of March due to the pandemic. Her husband still works at an insurance company; however, scaling down to one income has been challenging. “Things are a lot tighter. For the first time, we’re using programs like the Food Bank to save money,” Yvonne said. She said she loves the fresh fruits and veggies she gets from the school pantry in Oakland. While things are different and money is tight, Yvonne said she’s thankful she’s able to spend more time with her children. Setting up a daily schedule has helped them stay on track with school. “The food pantry has been a blessing,” she said. About Piedmont Council BSA The Piedmont Council has proudly served our community since 1910 when the first troop overnight event was held in Redwood Canyon in Oakland. The council was chartered eleven years later, in 1921. Although it is one of the smallest councils in the nation, it is widely recognized for its excellence and traditions of service and quality programs. Year after year more than 50% of the eligible youth in Piedmont participate in the council’s many programs. The growth of bilingual speakers in U.S. By Katie Pengilly More than half of the world’s population is bilingual, and the number of bilingual speakers in the U.S. is growing. So too is the body of research looking at the effects of bilingualism, which shows many cognitive advantages compared to monolingualism. Those include increased vocabulary, listening and reading skills, advanced problem solving, flexible thinking, and multi-tasking. In some cases, the bilingualism is forced, such as when a family moves to a country with a different language. In other instances, the bilingualism is optional, such as when a family decides to enroll their child in an immersion program in preschool or kindergarten. Simultaneous bilinguals learn two languages from birth, while sequential bilinguals learn a first language, and later introduce a second. Regardless of the specific circumstance, children have an enormous capacity for developing more than one language. With regard to supporting bilingual learners, the goal is simple: provide a high quantity of high-quality exposure to each language. The exact manner in which to accomplish this seems to be causing some confusion and conflicting advice to parents. For example, some parents are advised to take a structured approach based on a person, with one parent speaking one language and the other parent speaking the other. (In this situation, preference should be given to the language proficiency of each family member.) Some parents are advised to take a structured approach based on place, with one language spoken in the home and the other at school. And other families find a flexible use of both languages, without fixed rules, leads to balanced exposure and positive results. Some of the developmental guidelines for bilingual children also seem to be causing some confusion. Most bilingual children speak their first words by the time they are 1 year old, as is the case for monolingual children. Most bilingual children combine words into short phrases by the time they are 2 years old, as is the case with monolingual children. These early vocabulary words can be in one or both languages. As language develops, bilingual children may mix grammar rules, and/or use words from both languages within the same sentence. This is an entirely normal part of becoming a bilingual speaker. Some bilingual children, particularly sequential bilinguals, may not talk very much when they begin using their second language. This silent period may last several weeks or months and is also a normal part of becoming a bilingual speaker. I have regular conversations with parents regarding children who are exposed to multiple language, and are thinking that their children are “confused” or “delayed” due to multiple language exposure, or bilingualism. Bilingual children are not more likely than monolingual children to have difficulties with language, show delays in learning, or be diagnosed with a language disorder. But parent perceptions are often otherwise, revealing a disconnect from scientific findings. If a bilingual child is exhibiting symptoms of a speech, language and/or reading delay or difficulty, it will be evident in both languages, and should be evaluated by a professional. And if the child is not, parents should continue to provide a high quantity of high-quality exposure to each language. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. articles.text: When it became clear that Halloween activities would be curtailed this year, Piedmont parent Liz Mosbaugh went to work. She combined two of her passions -- creativity and fundraising for Piedmont schools -- to launch Piedmont BOO!, a socially-distanced, reverse trick-or-treat game. Starting on Saturday, October 17, Liz invited everyone in the community to sign up and purchase either a starter BOO! kit of a lawn sign, three BOO! count stickers, and access to the address list of other participants in the game, or the full BOO! kit which included the same supplies plus three complete BOO! bags filled with treats. Liz safely distributed the kits from her front yard with the help of her husband, Scott, and son, Chris. Participants would then “give a BOO!” by dropping a treat bag at the door of a participating home. When you received a surprise BOO!, you would place a round pumpkin sticker provided by Liz onto your colorful lawn sign. Once you received three BOO!s, you were done! Liz kept track of which homes still needed BOO!s on a handy map. Piedmont BOO! was a hit and Liz sold out of the lawn signs by October 28. All told, she put together 144 treat bags for 87 participating families, which raised more than $2,300 for the Piedmont Education Foundation and Piedmont schools. She

articles.text: Last week, Cub Scouts and other elementary-aged youth engaged in a fun virtual Twilight Camp. This annual camp, typically held in person over three days at Dracena Park, was done virtually this year. Kids enjoyed Halloween-themed crafts and snacks, they carved pumpkins, created mummy bookmarks, and participated in other fun activities. This threeday camp, traditionaly held in October prior to Halloween, was introduced in Piedmont by Deborah Aracic and quickly became a part of the Cub Scout program nationwide. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. articles.text: Continuing with COVIDsafe activities, Piedmont Scouts and leaders in Troop 4 recently went white-water rafting on the American River. To ensure health safety, the trip was organized around family “pods” rather than the normal scout patrols. Scouts cooked, camped and rafted with members of their families. The first afternoon was spent tubing and setting up camp. Later, the families made dinner and rested up for the big rafting day. “This is one of the Troop 4 scouts’ favorite annual trips. I’m glad we figured out a way to go safely this year,” said Scoutmaster Rob Rachwald. “Scouting has taken on special importance during quarantine by getting Troop 4 Scouts Jerry Yu (left) and Chris Li cook dinner for their families. The Rachwald family pod floating down the American River in October. The adventure brought many a smile to the scouts’ faces. Pictured are Troop 4 Scouts Jerry Yu (left) and Chris Li. scouts and adults into the great outdoors safely while showing you don’t need to be contained to your house.” His family pod included Scouts Lizzy and Peter Rachwald as well as his sister Inga and niece Maddie. Minfen Ding, the mother of Scout Jerry Yu, exclaimed, “This was the most fun trip ever for our group of eight since the pandemic. We all enjoyed the rafting, tubing and even jumping into the cold water.” For some families, part of the fun was going into the cold water, which the Frontiera-Dupree family got to experience when they tried to “surf” a rapid. Despite their involuntary swim, everyone was okay and back on their way in no time. “This was a very special weekend for the Scouts because they got to enjoy an outdoor adventure that was COVID-safe. They are still talking about it. My goal for Troop 4 is to make sure we can keep active and safe,” said Scoutmaster Walter Stokes. Troop 4 is recruiting. Families with sons and daughters who are looking for adventure are encouraged to contact Sarah King (sarahdmertz@yahoo.com) for details. The Stokes family was all smiles amidst the white water and rapids in the American River. articles.text: “The Sky’s the Limit” exhibition includes 72 paintings At a time when beauty has never been more important, come be a part of the resilience of the arts. The one element in a painting that can have the greatest impact on the perception of atmosphere is sky. The types of colors used, the cloud composition, the quality of brush stroke....these are some of the details that can effect a viewer’s perception of sky. But this was not always the case. In the world of French classical painting, for instance, the landscape was a mere backdrop for some tale from antiquity or a scene from the Bible. It wasn’t until the late 1700’s that we see greater emphasis on sky: horizon lines dropped as artists began to explore greater variations in the rendering of sky. Indeed, in some art, sky was no longer a backdrop, but rather became the subject. Join artist and art historian Michael Stehr as he presents a zoom lecture to lead us on an examination of sky in painting. This lecture will also serve to open his current exhibition, “The Sky’s the Limit!” Michael will also describe his own approach to rendering variable skies. articles.text: Piedmont native Mackenzie McDonald has powered his way to the quarterfinals of two recent tournaments, the Istanbul Challenger Open from October 18-23, and the Astana Open in Khazakstan from October 28-October 30. This comes after being knocked out in the second round of the French Open on September 30 by No. 1 ranked Rafael Nadal in three sets, 6-1, 6-0, 6-3, and a first-round loss to Alexander Bublik in the St. Petersburg Open on October 12. McDonald has been a man on a mission since those losses, jumping in the ranking from No. 236 to No. 191. McDonald’s highest ATP ranking was No. 57 in April 2019, but a hamstring injury and subsequent surgery caused him to miss the entire 2019 season and training as well. “It took a really serious team and a lot of hard work. The surgery was pretty big. I have a masPhotos courtesy of ATPTour.com Piedmont native Mackenzie McDonald reached the quarterfinals of his last two ATP tour competitions. sive scar underneath my butt and I wasn’t able to walk for the first month-and-a-half, two months. Time was going by really slowly,” McDonald said, via ATPTour. com. Mackenzie McDonald defeated No. 49 ranked Alexander Bublik in the Astana Open in Khazakstan, marking a turnaround from a loss to him in St. Petersburg. At the Istanbul ATP Challenger he competed in five matches, entering as the topranked entrant of the qualifiers. He defeated Felipe Meligini Rodrigues Alves (3-6, 6-1, 6-3) and Viktor Galovic (6-2, 6-4) to reach the Round of 32. In the first round of the knockout stages, McDonald took down Teymuraz Gabashvili in straight sets, 6-4, 6-1. In the Round of 16, the Pride of Piedmont won again in straight sets over Nino Serdausic 7-6 (9), 6-3. The first set finished in a heated 10-point superbreaker which went backand-forth to an extra 11th point. In the quarterfinals, McDonald lost to No. 149 ranked Martin Klizan 4-6, 6-4, 6-3. At the Astana Open in Khazakstan, McDonald won in straight sets, 6-3, 6-2, in a rematch with Bublik, who entered as the sixth seed in the ladder in the Round of 32 and ranked No. 49 among ATP players. It was McDonald’s biggest win since returning from injury. In th ematch, McDonald powered his first serve into play on 37 of 49 attempts for a sparkling 76 percent conversion rate. He won points on 27 of them despite making only gaining one ace. He also did well on returns, converting 36 of 69 points (52 percent). He went on to take down No. 103 ranked Andreas Seppi in the Round of 16 in similar fashion, winning 36 of 55 first-serve points, a stellar 65 percent, while getting the ball into play on 55 of 87 first serves – notching seven aces this time. McDonald finished the tourament after losing 6-1, 6-4 to No. 36 ranked Adrian Mannarino in the quarterfinals.

articles.text: As Piedmont begins to get its high school sports programs back (at least online), hope trickles its way back into town. The hope is that fraternity, exercise, socialization and above all, distraction, will bring some pep to the steps of the city’s young athletes and their fans. The revival of professional sports in the last few months made for some soap opera-worthy drama. The NBA moved for an extended stay in a “bubble” at Disney World. Major League Baseball changed its rules: extra innings saw a runner start the inning on base, and double-headers turned into seven-inning games. Baseball’s postseason took place at empty neutral sites littered with teddy bears, and cardboard cutoffs of fans, dogs and even Bernie from the movie Weekend at Bernie’s. It turned out that Los Angeles won both the NBA and MLB championships. Although this reporter does not ever brandish the black and orange of the S.F. Giants, seeing Los Angeles succeed at anything is terribly upsetting. Nobody outside of L.A. can tolerate L.A., right? Or am I projecting? On the bright side, the Los Angeles Angels and Los Angeles Clippers did not win their leagues. So, think about this – in one way, L.A. loses every year by having multiple teams. At any rate, the opening of sports did bring back a modicum of distraction to fans across the globe. Having something to watch and something on a calendar brings much needed familiarity, tradition and relief. In-person attendance has all but been nixed – except for limited capacity at 13 games in the MLB postseason, and limited attendance at some NFL stadiums. The joy of going to a pro sporting event in person was acutely absent this summer. The Coliseum, Oracle stadium, the new Chase Center, and the Raider’s brand-new Death Star stadium in Vegas have been oh, so lonely. No mustard loaded hot dogs have rolled downstairs, nor have any tragic beer spills hit the bleachers. No seats have been played like drums, and the decibels from crowd noise have not hit triple digits. Things could have been much worse, though. If a pro athlete were to get deathly ill with COVID-19 with permanent damage, what was to happen? Season canceled, right? That contingency was not explicitly disseminated to the public. Luckily that did not happen, even in the NFL where maybe one third of the league’s players are over 300 pounds. Obesity increases the chance of serious COVID cases. But so far, so good in the world of pro sports. At least the cheating Houston Astros did not make the World Series. A championship by the Asterisks of Houston would have left a foul taste in the mouths of many. It would have been a taste that not even the “loss of taste” COVID-19 symptom could have altered. Back home, equipped with a new and spirited Athletic Director, youthful, energetic Bradley Smet, Piedmont is preparing to bring back some masked, in-person, distanced and outdoor workouts for its sports teams. Tennis, as a naturally socially-distance sport, has already been practicing in the afternoons. Other teams will expand their digital workouts through Zoom and Google Meet. Water polo players have enjoyed collectively working out as a team for some weeks, though without water – the basis of their existence. Sure, there is increased risk by bringing athletes back in person, but people need something, and sports can certainly be that something. As we collectively but unsuccessfully have been trying to say “goodbye COVID” for more than seven months, now at least we can say “Go Highlanders!”

OPINION And the crowd goes silent By Jay Russell As Piedmont begins to get its high school sports programs back (at least online), hope trickles its way back into town. The hope is that fraternity, exercise, socialization and above all, distraction, will bring some pep to the steps of the city’s young athletes and their fans. The revival of professional sports in the last few months made for some soap opera-worthy drama. The NBA moved for an extended stay in a “bubble” at Disney World. Major League Baseball changed its rules: extra innings saw a runner start the inning on base, and double-headers turned into seven-inning games. Baseball’s postseason took place at empty neutral sites littered with teddy bears, and cardboard cutoffs of fans, dogs and even Bernie from the movie Weekend at Bernie’s. It turned out that Los Angeles won both the NBA and MLB championships. Although this reporter does not ever brandish the black and orange of the S.F. Giants, seeing Los Angeles succeed at anything is terribly upsetting. Nobody outside of L.A. can tolerate L.A., right? Or am I projecting? On the bright side, the Los Angeles Angels and Los Angeles Clippers did not win their leagues. So, think about this – in one way, L.A. loses every year by having multiple teams. At any rate, the opening of sports did bring back a modicum of distraction to fans across the globe. Having something to watch and something on a calendar brings much needed familiarity, tradition and relief. In-person attendance has all but been nixed – except for limited capacity at 13 games in the MLB postseason, and limited attendance at some NFL stadiums. The joy of going to a pro sporting event in person was acutely absent this summer. The Coliseum, Oracle stadium, the new Chase Center, and the Raider’s brand-new Death Star stadium in Vegas have been oh, so lonely. No mustard loaded hot dogs have rolled downstairs, nor have any tragic beer spills hit the bleachers. No seats have been played like drums, and the decibels from crowd noise have not hit triple digits. Things could have been much worse, though. If a pro athlete were to get deathly ill with COVID-19 with permanent damage, what was to happen? Season canceled, right? That contingency was not explicitly disseminated to the public. Luckily that did not happen, even in the NFL where maybe one third of the league’s players are over 300 pounds. Obesity increases the chance of serious COVID cases. But so far, so good in the world of pro sports. At least the cheating Houston Astros did not make the World Series. A championship by the Asterisks of Houston would have left a foul taste in the mouths of many. It would have been a taste that not even the “loss of taste” COVID-19 symptom could have altered. Back home, equipped with a new and spirited Athletic Director, youthful, energetic Bradley Smet, Piedmont is preparing to bring back some masked, in-person, distanced and outdoor workouts for its sports teams. Tennis, as a naturally socially-distance sport, has already been practicing in the afternoons. Other teams will expand their digital workouts through Zoom and Google Meet. Water polo players have enjoyed collectively working out as a team for some weeks, though without water – the basis of their existence. Sure, there is increased risk by bringing athletes back in person, but people need something, and sports can certainly be that something. As we collectively but unsuccessfully have been trying to say “goodbye COVID” for more than seven months, now at least we can say “Go Highlanders!” ADVERTISE IN THE POST

articles.text: San Francisco Conservatory of Music will celebrate Beethoven’s birthday with a mini-concert on Saturday, November 14. The concert, to be performed in Sol Joseph Recital Hall, will be available online and can be viewed from home. The mini-festival will feature Beethoven’s rarely performed, but still magnificent vocal works. The celebration of the 250th anniversary of Beethoven’s birth is presented by the San Francisco Conservatory of Music’s Historical Performance department. Included will be rarely heard vocal works, including solo songs, vocal duet and trios from Eight Songs, Op. 52 (1790-96), Six Songs, Op. 75 (1809), Four Ariettas and a Duet (1809), Three Songs, Op. 83 (1810), and arrangements of Scottish and Irish folk songs for voice, violin, cello and piano (1810-1818). The event is curated by Corey Jamason, Chair of the conservatory’s Historical Performances department. Sign up to receive a livestream link the day of the concert. Visit https://sfcm.edu/ performance-calendar/event/fallbaroque-voice-concert to sign up.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young hosts a series of free online musical gatherings entitled “Joseph Young and Friends,” which will conclude on November 19 with a look to the future. The final episode of the series offers a look into Berkeley Symphony’s future programs, by showcasing composers Brian Raphael Nabors and Jimmy Lopez. New Music USA recently announced a new commissioning project with Nabors and Berkeley Symphony. “This collaboration is important to me on so many levels and brings to life a vision that I have had since entering this industry,” Young said. “It has always been a goal of mine to champion composers that look like me, that speak to the range of today’s experiences, and that can offer diverse perspectives for our audiences. It is essential to provide a platform for composers to create openly and freely with limited parameters so that they can bring unique color and life to the ever-growing musical canon. Berkeley Symphony has a rich history of commissioning new works, and this collaboration with New Music USA will continue to shape the discovery of emerging composers through long term relationships between the composer, the orchestra, and our beloved community.” Nabors, originally from Birmingham, Alabama, is a composer of emotionally enriching music that tells exciting narratives with its vibrant themes and colorful harmonic language. Nabors draws from combinations of Jazz Funk, R&B, and Gospel. His music has been performed by the Cincinnati, Atlanta, Nashville, and Detroit Symphony Orchestras. He is a 2020 Fulbright scholarship University of Cincinnati Conservatory of Music. “This project is impactful in so many ways. I am beyond honored and elated to share and serve as a voice for so many who look like me and share my experience,” Nabors said. “Along with my wonderful colleagues, I believe this ground breaking work will help to lay the foundation for barriers to be broken and the eradication of stigmas that have plagued our field for many years. To be a part of that change is an affirmation of everything I’ve worked for and continue to work for. Watch the final episode at https://www.berkeleysymphony. org/joseph-young-friends/. articles.text: Meryl Streep and Amy Adams star in Julie and Julia. Movie review by Chris Honoré What is there to say to those who have not seen Julie and Julia but bon appetit! This film. Made in 2009, is a joy to watch, a celebration of Julia (Meryl Streep) and Julie (Amy Adams), two women who embrace life and manage to square the compass and find in cooking, in the preparation of sauces and chicken and lobster, a happiness that up to that point proved elusive. The film blends two books, My Life in France, a memoir by Julia Child, and Julie and Julia, a book by Julie Powell. Through seamless editing th film offers a glimpse into the live of both women as they struggle to master the art of French cooking. In the opening scene Julia and her husband Paul (Stanley Tucci) arrive in post-war France where he is posted as an American Cultural Attache’. Julia, feeling at a loss, enrolls in a French cooking school and unexpectedly, surprisingly, discovers she has a talent as well as a passion for cooking. The film then jumps ahead to 2002, and introduces Julie Powell, a frustrated writer, stuck in a confining office job, who decides to cook all the recipes in Child’s cookbook, Mastering the Art of French Cooking, and keep a daily blog of her experiences. Writrer Nora Ephron masterfully weaves the two parallel lives together, separated by 50 years, and directs a wonderful recipe for one of her best films to date. Of the many wonderful performances in Julie and Julia, we must begin with the role of Maryl Streep, who simply inhabits the character of Child. It is a stunning transformation. Child was a large and generous personality, effusive and expressive, hooting and laughing to the point of caricature. But never, not for a moment does Streep allow her character to become any more or less than deeply human and transfixing and completely Julia. It’s an unparalleled performance, subtle, nuanced and comic, one that is breathtaking in its craftsmanship. Ditto for the incomparable Tucci. He is masterful, nurturing constantly the chemistry between Julia and himself, able to speak volumes with one expression, capable of being absolutely still as a scene develops around him (recall his sterling performance in The Devil Wore Prada, where he was first teamed with Streep). As well, Amy Adams, playing against Streep, though they never meet, is perfect as the neophyte who bubbles with passion for the art of a recipe and reacts to every obstacle with emotion that is authentic and spot on. She is a consummate actress. If there is undiluted joy to be found in film, Nora Ephron has captured it in this very special movie. Julie and Julia. Starring Meryl Streep, Amy Adams, Stanley Tucci, Jane Lynch and Chris Messina. Written and Directed by Nora Ephron. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Julie and Julia a masterful film about cooking – and Julia Child

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Before you see Adrift, resist the temptation to learn anything about the story and the overwhelming events that frame act three. The narrative is in two stories. The first is a love story between two kindred spirits, Tami Oldham (Shailene Woodley) and Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin). Both twenty-something. The year is 1983. The place Tahiti. Tami, who left her home in San Diego right out of high school, began to drift from port to port throughout the South Pacific, working odd jobs, crewing on boats and tourist ships. Newly arrived in Tahiti, she meets New Zealander Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), who has just arrived on his trim 36-foot schooner, the Mayaluga. Almost immediately they begin a relationship, nurtured by the gorgeous beaches, long sails on Richard’s boat, strolls through outdoor marketplaces, awash in color. All is kissed by soft trade winds gently blowing through. The two relish being together, with lives that share a world view that embraces an existence far off the grid. Of course, Richard asks Tami to join him in his travels and they plan their sail from Tahiti to places east. Unexpectedly, Richard meets two fellow sailors from London who propose to hire him to sail their spectacular boat, with all the possible comforts available on a 45-footer, from Tahiti to San Diego, Tami’s hometown. The offer is sweetened with $10,000 and two firstclass airplane tickets back to Tahiti after the boat is delivered. The money, Tami and Richard conclude, could keep them sailing for at least a year, and they decide to leave the Mayaluga in Tahiti and make the trip. And so begins act three, the most intense part of the film. This is a compellingly entertaining film, and is especially well-acted by Shailene Woodley who is most convincing. As full disclosure: I love sailing movies. I love the idea of sails filled with wind and the absolute silence, other than the sound of halyards banging softly against the mast, or waves hitting the bow and sending up a welcoming spray that reaches the cockpit. I spent a lot of time doing this on San Francisco Bay out by Alcatraz and over by Tiburon, with Sausalito in the distance. But blue water sailing is profoundly more difficult – something Adrift graphically conveys. Know that you don’t ever need to have stepped topside on a teak deck to become lost in Adrift. It’s an amazing film. Adrift. Directed by Baltasar Kormakur. Starring Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp star in Adrift.

Movie review by Chris Honoré Grave of Fireflies is a must-see if you have been captured by the extraordinary animation and storytelling that has come to define Studio Ghibli. It is, without hesitation, an achingly beautiful film that transcends all expectations. Know, however, that the story is profoundly sad and emotive. Because it is animated, and its two main characters are children, it is easy to assume that its subject matter will reflect the fanciful innocence associated with the animé genre. But while the film is an allegory of sorts, it also challenges our assumptions about animation. Grave of Fireflies is set in Kobe, Japan. The year is 1945, and World War II is coming to a close, despite the unwillingness of the Japanese to stand down. Told in a long flashback, the tale focuses on a 14-year-old boy named Seita (J. Robert Spencer) and his 5-year-old sister, Setsuko (Rhoda Chrosite). Orphaned by allied fire-bombings, their mother killed, they go to live with their aunt (Amy Jones) whose initial charitable response to the children turns surprisingly bitter. Seita finally decides that they must leave. The two find a cave in the hills and for a brief time all is well. But before long malnutrition stalks them. Seita is beaten while looking for food and Setsuko falls ill. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Inside Out. Film review by Chris Honoré The idea comprising the essence of Pixar’s Inside Out is inspired. The filmmakers, who have a long and solid resume of animated films (Up, Wall-E, Toy Story, Finding Nemo), are able to confront the third dimension in movies because they can. This is, after all, a world in which animators can take a step that otherwise would be impossible in a photographed feature. Here’s what they did: knowing that a filmed narrative cannot penetrate a character’s mind (except, perhaps, using voice over), they tell a familiar story of an 11-year-old girl named Riley (Kaitlyn Dias). She lives happily in the embrace of her parents in Minnesota, has loads of friends and plays on a hockey team. For Riley life is better than good. That is until her father takes a new job and they must relocate to San Francisco. Up until this point, Riley’s default setting is contentment and joy – school, friends, sports all fit into a much-enjoyed spectrum of childhood on the cusp of being a teenager (Riley defines the word tween). With the impending move, Riley’s world is rocked. She is confronted with challenges that are new to her. Her new house is a bit grim, as is her neighborhood. She tries out for hockey and it doesn’t go well. Suddenly Riley begins to slide into a funk. And though her parents ask her if everything is all right (of course, Riley grumbles that all is fine), the emotions taking place inside are a different story. Here is where the Pixar storytellers create another world. They craft a kind of emotional wheelhouse (in Riley’s head) that includes all of Riley’s emotions. It’s wonderful. There’s Joy (Amy Poehler), Fear (Bill Hader), Anger (Lewis Black), Disgust (Mindy Kaling) and Sadness (Phyllis Smith). Each is a unique and funny and engaging character, and all are coping with Riley’s new world and a bevy of feelings that are at first decidedly unsettling. Riley has always been encouraged to be happy. To smile. But then she has been grounded in a spiffy life. Hence Joy, vivacious and energetic, has always had her hand on the tiller, suddenly Anger and Fear and Sadness (most especially) find that their roles in Riley’s emotions are growing. Meanwhile, Joy, becomes lost in a labyrinth of Riley’s mind and must struggle to find its way back to emotion central before things get really awful for Riley. You have to see this crew in action – Anger is a squat, redfaced, short-fused guy – to have a complete understanding of what Pixar has accomplished. It tells a compelling story, one that kids will relate to and one that adults will quickly recognize . . Growth is dealing with the internal dialogue that takes place all of our lives. This may be Riley’s first experience with an unfamiliar spectrum of emotions, but it won’t be her last. And beginning on the journey of dealing with the crew up in the wheelhouse, to include Sadness and Fear and Anger, as well as Joy, she must make choices and sort out some stuff. Of course, it’s all a central if imperfect part of life. It’s also the meaning of that lifelong process called “growing up”, something that Riley eventually comes to realize. Watch for the credits. They’re terrific. As is Inside Out. Inside Out. Animated from Pixar Animation Studios and Walt Disney Pictures. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG. Released in 2015.
articles.title: Inside Out a marvel of animated moviemaking

articles.text: The California Society of Printmakers’ 106th Exhibition will be held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from November 15 to December 5. As part of the wide range of art offered at the Center throughout the year, the Society of Printmakers exhibition is an annual show. It highlights a variety of printmaking techniques and the ways its member artists use many techniques to create unique and meaningful works of art. The Society’s mission is to support the integrity of traditional printmaking while providing a community for artists exploring new directions in contemporary print methods. articles.text: Josef Haydn portrait by Ludwig Guttenbrunn Very few composers changed the course of music. The list is short. In chronological order they were Haydn, Beethoven, Paganini, Berlioz, Wagner, and Stravinsky. That’s about it. The main reason is that music is the most conservative of all the arts, and thus is the last to change directions. The graphic arts innovate first. They are happy flinging paint on a canvas. But music continues like the meandering of an old river. The rapids are few. In many ways, music is reactive. It is the last of the arts to change. Josef Haydn is the first composer to figure prominently as an innovator. It is interesting to consider the similarities between Haydn and Beethoven. People often think of Ludwig von Beethoven as the stupendous creator. To this, musicologists counter that Haydn did it long before Beethoven. Haydn established the tradition. He invented the string quartet and the symphony. Beethoven then took it to the iconoclast level – and in this he was perfect. We must keep in mind that Beethoven always lamented that the public never really understood him. They saw him as strange and eccentric. He was, however, the epitome of humanity, both personally and musically. All of the composers on this list were sensitive and generous. You might ask, what about Wagner? Yes, he fits the definition, but only in his own way. The next innovator was the French composer Hector Berlioz. His cataclysmic Symphonie Fantastique came only five years after the death of Beethoven. Berlioz painted his musical canvases with a completely new palette. Richard Wagner’s contributions to music are often considered the greatest of all. He unified all elements of music with drama and stage production. The most recent innovator was the Russian-born Igor Stravinsky. Like Beethoven, Stravinsky threw tradition out the window, then retrieved what society viewed as reprehensible and flung it in the face of tradition. He was a master of that… Like no one before. But the most sensational by far was Niccolò Paganini. In fact, he was the most sensational entertainer of all time. This is no exaggeration. Music is delineated by Paganini. When he arrived, the entire musical world changed. Paganini’s genius drew on all those violinists who came before him. He assimilated everything and then blazed a trail that no one had ever taken. He was, in every way, the embodiment of the modern performer – absolutely a trail-blazing virtuoso. He was also the prototype of the media-wise public figure. It was Paganini, in fact, who was the inventor of the publicity machine. Every entertainer since Paganini has modeled the media blitz after him. Last week, October 27, was Paganini’s birthday. It is interesting to note that Jascha Heifetz’s earth-shattering debut in Carnegie Hall was also on October 27 (1917). Historical recordings can be a revealing time machine. A recent release enabled me to relive a memorable concert of September 1, 1963. It was a gala concert in the Hollywood Bowl featuring Jascha Heifetz on violin, Gregor Piatigorsky on cello, and Leonard Bernstein conducting the New York Philharmonic. They performed the Brahms double concerto. What a different musical world it was back then. Those musicians were titans – so elevated from the terrestrial which passes as genius today. Standing ovations were earned back then, and Heifetz and Piatigorsky got a standing ovation at that September concert. I left the performance imagining myself in heaven. How wonderful it is to relive that experience.

articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players’ virtual series, Bach Shorts, will end on November 8 with a performance by Robert Howard. Howard, a cellist from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonic Baroque Orchestra, will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. He will also perform select movements from Suites #1, 2, and 3. Bach Connections is the final piece of three performances in the Bach Shorts series. Bach Shorts are one hour, live-streamed performances that seek to connect us through an intimate exploration of The Six Cello Suites by J.S. Bach. The series showcased performances by two prominent Bay Area cellists, Christopher Costanza and Jennifer Kloetzel, and will conclude next month with Howard. The performance will stream live via YouTube on Sunday, November 8, at 4 p.m. To obtain tickets in advance, visit https:// app.ar ts-people.com /index. php?show=116151.

articles.text: Gowns from the Die Fledermaus show will be available to purchase at this year’s San Francisco Opera costume sale. San Francisco Opera will have its first costume sale online from Friday to Sunday, November 13-15. The annual costume sale, which was moved to online this year due to the coronavirus, features individually designed outfits direct from the opera stage. Each costume carries a piece of San Francisco Opera history and was made locally in the Bay Area by a team of talented artists, craftspeople and costume designers. Unleash your inner warrior with costumes designed for fantasy dramas like Tannhäuser; or party like there’s no tomorrow with the ornate jackets and gowns of Die Fledermaus and The Merry Widow. Make sure to peruse through the size chart, available on the opera’s website, because costumes are often custom-made and are not traditionally sized. In the past, the opera’s costume shop sale has been one of the most anticipated events by patrons and the general public. Proceeds from this year’s sale will benefit the San Francisco Opera and support general operating expenses including artist support, young artist development, and educational programs. To see the costumes that will be on sale, visit https://sfopera. com/opera-is-on/costumesale/.

articles.text: Piedmont, like much of California, is blessed with what is considered a temperate Mediterranean climate – often perfect for outdoor activities. To take advantage of this we create different kinds of outdoor spaces, everything from nature parks to improved sports fields to smaller contained areas for dining, socializing, or just relaxing. These latter spaces are often referred to as “outdoor rooms” in architectural jargon. While the exact description of an outdoor room is a little vague, there are a number of characteristics that help define this type of space, examples of which become recognizable when walking through town. I think the chief characteristic of an outdoor room is often referred to as a sense of enclosure, resembling in a certain way a “room” without a roof. Why a feeling of enclosure makes an outdoor space appealing and comfortable is difficult to define. Maybe it is a mixture of privacy, security, a feeling of boundary to a more developed space or simply the designation of a definitive area for a certain use, like the BBQ terrace or the dining patio. This enclosure is often made up of the exterior walls of an adjoining building. Higher planting, shrubbery, landscape walls or even trees can also form or contribute to these “walls” that form enclosure. articles.text: Working from home for eight months at this point, and into the foreseeable future, has meant preparing lunch at home too. Most days I cobble together a plate of leftovers, but sometimes making lunch from scratch is the way to go. Eating out for lunch was my previous norm, and a San Francisco FiDi office meant there was no shortage of variety and options. Since I do WFH, any lunch I prepare from scratch has to be fast, and with ingredients on hand. Variety is a small pleasure too. The short start-to-finish of this satisfying bowl of noodle soup also means you can have it in your rotation for whenever you need a quick and easy meal – lunch or dinner. This recipe puts together a handful of pantry and ‘fridge staples, with endless substitutions for variety. Any noodle will work: soba, ramen, udon, rice sticks or spaghetti. Similarly, to “doctor” the broth, try flavor profiles from Central and Southeast Asia using curry powders or prepared pastes. These days there are many options in broths and flavors. You may find ones that require little to no “doctoring” for an easier means to a delicious end. I am already thinking of a Thai-style version by adding a splash of coconut milk and a spoonful of prepared curry paste, red or green; and adding shrimp for protein. The recipe below is a guide based on one serving, but it scales easily according to the number of servings desired, and heft of the appetites involved. It’s perfect for a quick dinner too. Soba Noodle Soup with Salmon and Broccoli Makes one hearty bowl INGREDIENTS For each serving: • 2 cups chicken broth, or preferred substitute • 1-1/2 ounces dried soba noodles • 3 ounces cooked salmon • 1/2 cup broccoli flowerets • 1/4 cup fresh mushrooms, sliced, optional • 1 green onion, sliced thin • 1/2 teaspoon soy sauce, to taste • 1/4 teaspoon toasted sesame seed oil • Pinch of powdered ginger, or a few of freshly grated • Pinch of granulated garlic, or a few of freshly grated • Pinch of ground white pepper • Sprinkle of shichimi togarashi, Japanese chili spice mix, to taste INSTRUCTIONS In a medium saucepan, boil the soba noodles according to package directions, except stop cooking just shy of done. They will continue cooking a bit while you prepare the broth. The brand I use calls for four minutes’ cooking time, I stop at about three minutes. Drain the soba noodles in a strainer and transfer to a prewarmed serving bowl. Make sure to use a generously sized bowl to assure everything fits. In the same saucepan, combine the broth, soy sauce, toasted sesame oil, ginger, garlic and white pepper to taste; and bring to a low boil. Add the broccoli and mushrooms (if using) and cook until just tender. Add the cooked salmon to reheat it. Add the salmon, broccoli and mushrooms to the soba noodles and then pour the hot broth over. Garnish with green onions and add shichimi togarashi, or other chili seasoning to taste. articles.text: Barbara Jean Borsuk, a resident of Piedmont for more than 60 years, passed away peacefully surrounded by her family on September 19, 2020. She was 97. Born Barbara Jean Bacharach on October 28, 1922 in Oakland, she was the daughter of Percy and Etta Bacharach. She graduated from Lowell High School in San Francisco. and married Sidney Borsuk after World War II. A short while later they moved to Piedmont. Barbara firmly believed in education, and at age 63 she earned a bachelor’s degree in art at Holy Names University. Besides being active in her family’s real estate business, Barbara owned and managed a toy shop on Piedmont Avenue in the 1980s, which piqued her interest in designing dollhouses and miniatures. Barbara and Sidney had terrific adventures together, traveling the world, entertaining, and going on family vacations. They especially loved treating their family to annual vacations in Maui over the holidays. Barbara remained a very active woman in her 90s, but her husband Sidney, the love of her life, died in 2005 at age 90 after 59 years of marriage. Barbara had many interests, including painting, tennis and golf. She was a member of the Oakland Hills Tennis Club. Throughout her life she provided support to local charities and community organizations, including the former Oakland Ballet, Oakland Symphony, and the Jewish Welfare Fund and Danville’s Jewish Home for the Aged. She volunteered for 26 years at the American Cancer SociBarbara Borsuk and husband Sidney at a formal event. ety’s Discovery retail shop on Piedmont Avenue and as a docent at the Oakland Museum of California. She is survived by her son, Mark and his wife Liliane, and by her daughter, Suzanne Borsuk and Suzanne’s children, Garrett Krueger and his wife Allyson, and daughters Sydney Krueger and Andrea Krueger. articles.text: David Maglaty, FAIA, 70, died at home in Piedmont with his family by his side on October 16, 2020. He spent the last year of his life with his family and friends, biking, walking and visiting in between treatments for prostate cancer. Born on June 29, 1950 in Hartford, Connecticut, David Cook Maglaty was the son of Esther Lila (Cook) Maglaty and Mario Louis Maglaty. David and his siblings Lois and Mark were raised in West Hartford where he attended school until college. In 1977 he graduated with a Bachelor of Architecture from the University of Oregon in Eugene. David met his wife, Jean Hansen, at Ratcliff Architects in Berkeley in July 1979. A lifelong runner, David’s days began with coffee, followed most days by a 5-7 mile run. He ran his first marathon shortly after his daughter’s birth, followed by some triathlons, and many 5K races, often competing with his neighbor and fellow runner, Steve Sidney. David was a consummate architect. Ever investigating the context and site for each project, working closely with the communities and clients where his projects were built, he explored design options with a skilled pencil or pen. He brought to life sketches that are today considered accomplished works in themselves, inspirations for many projects that were built, and some not. David is remembered for many projects, often on college campuses and the communities they serve. Close to home, his design of student infill housing for UC Berkeley, Units 1 and 2, on College Avenue and Durant Street, illustrates his idea that social space plays an important role and ultimately fosters a safer community environment. David’s work received numerous awards over the years, including the prestigious AIA National Honor Award in 2008 for the Units 1 and 2, Infill Student Housing at UC Berkeley (EHDD), as well as the AIA Santa Clara in 2012 and San Francisco Honor Award in 2013 David Maglaty, an architect and athlete, died at home on October 16. He was 70. for the Orchard School Library in San Jose (HMC). David was named a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects in 2014. David and Jean raised their children, Alissa and Peter, in Piedmont and he cherished them, appreciating every moment shared. He coached soccer for both kids’ teams and was a pack leader for Peter’s Cub Scout and Boy Scout troops. Father and son enjoyed high Sierra backpacking trips every year through high school with Troop 15. David is survived by his best friend and wife of 39 years, Jean Hansen, daughter, Alissa Maglaty and son, Peter Maglaty. He will be greatly missed by his sister, Lois McCabe and brother, Mark Maglaty; and his many beloved in-laws, walking buddies, fellow runners, colleagues and friends. The family is indebted to the staff at Kaiser Permanente, Oakland, especially their oncology department, palliative and hospice staff. They became a part of the family, and we so appreciate their regimens that kept David comfortable this past year. To attend a celebration/memorial, please contact the family at remembering.david.maglaty@ gmail.com. To make a contribution in memory of David that supports cancer research for Bay Area fire fighters and families, go to San Francisco Firefighters Cancer Prevention Foundation, https:// www.sffcpf.org/

articles.text: Jim Adams, a Piedmont native, passed away far too early of natural causes on October 23, 2020 at his home in San Francisco. He spent his last few days at his beloved family home in Glenbrook, Nevada, with beautiful, sunny Fall weather and sunsets that were “epic”. He was 58. Born James Thomas Adams on Groundhog Day, February 2, 1962, he was the son of Thomas and Sally Adams. He spent a happy childhood in Piedmont, with his older siblings, Julie and Mike. He attended Piedmont High School where he made lifelong friends through football, rugby, Rigma Lions and the Hagglund’s Hackers Championship basketball team. He graduated in 1980 and attended Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo. He graduated from San Francisco State with a bachelor’s degree in Journalism. He settled in San Francisco and began a career as a stock brofamily. He even checked Punxatawney, PA off of his bucket list and saw the Groundhog at dawn on his birthday. Jim enjoyed all things outdoors – from fly fishing to duck hunting and especially scuba diving. He loved to simply watch the ocean and look for whales. And they all agree that the secret to keeping a tree fresh is to obsess – be obsessive about the water level. It’s yes to glitter, toppers and white lights, but no food on the tree. It has something to do with homemade gingerbread ornaments and ants, needless to say, the ornaments were off-limits to the children. articles.text: Piedmont’s annual Turkey Trot on Thanksgiving morning will have a distinctly different look this year. Covid-19 has thrown the world into a sticky mess - not unlike a kitchen sink after Thanksgiving dinner. Given Alameda County health directives, the Piedmont Turkey Trot will not be held live this year. However, the Trot is putting its best shank forward and will carry on the spirit of the Trot – virtually in 2020. While we can’t physically gather as usual to celebrate what would be the 19th Annual Trot amidst the beautiful fall colors on the lovely roads of Piedmont, we can still trot amongst ourselves this Thanksgiving – physically-distanced, but virtually-united. The Piedmont Turkey Trot Challenge will be a virtual scavenger hunt. Register online at piedmontturkeytrot.com and then run or walk the streets of Piedmont to find the PTT lawn signs in various gardens around town. Snap a selfie with the sign, upload to our Instagram account @piedmontturkeytrot, and be automatically entered into a drawing for prizes. Each Instagram posting from a registered participant is an official entry. The more signs you find, the more opportunities you will have to win. If you are looking to move your feet a little faster, participants may also choose to run their favorite 5K route on their own or in family pods, then upload their 5K time for bragging rights at their (smaller, yet mighty) Thanksgiving table. Lawn signs will be up from November 15 to November 29. Registration is $10. See you on Instagram!

articles.text: Alameda County remains in Orange Tier for reopening of businesses Four more cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont during the past seven days, according to information from the Alameda County Public Health Department yesterday, Tuesday, November 3. In total, 47 cases now have been reported in the City since the coronavirus pandemic began in March. Overall in Alameda County, the weekly positive percentage for COVID-19 tests is currently 1.6 percent, a slight uptick compared to recent weeks. The number of new cases countywide has crept upward in recent days, although figures are well below numbers in August. Yesterday, there were 55 new cases in the county. On August 13, the worst day yet for the county, there were 421 new cases. Overall, the caseload in Alameda County is 24,162, an increase of over 500 cases from one week ago. The county has recorded 466 total COVID-19 fatalities. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 9,273. In Hayward, 3,565 cases have been recorded and there have been 1,700 reported in Fremont. San Leandro has reported 1,359 and Livermore reported 1,028. Alameda County updated its shelter-in-place order on Friday, October 23 that reflect the county’s status as an Orange Tier county. According to California’s reopening system, the Orange Tier is the second-least restrictive tier for reopening the economy. The state placed Alameda County into the Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, on October 13. Indoor dining is now allowed, but capacity must be restricted to 25 percent or 100 people, whichever is fewer. Restaurant owners are not rushing to reopen indoors, many choosing to continue with outdoor dining. Bowling alleys, indoor worship services, movie theaters and gyms can reopen, all with capacity restrictions. Capacity restrictions for indoor retail and malls have been increased to 50 percent. Alameda County’s new cases per day remains too high for the county to meet benchmarks for the Yellow Tier, or Minimal Tier. The county is recording an average of 3.2 cases per 100,000 people. A county must have 1 case per 100,000 or fewer to be in the Yellow Tier. San Francisco is the only county in the Bay Area currently in the Yellow Tier. As of press time, 934,672 cases of COVID-19 have been recorded in California. There have been 17,686 deaths due to the disease statewide.

articles.text: Piedmont police arrested a man sleeping in his car at 6:34 a.m. one day before Halloween when he was found to have an outstanding $10,000 warrant out of Alameda County for a parole violation of Grand Theft. After receiving a call about a suspicious vehicle, the police interviewed and arrested Anthony Smith, 31, a transient, who was in a silver Mercedes parked on Oakland Avenue. Smith was on probation for grand theft and carrying a loaded firearm in public. Officers arrested Smith and transported him to Santa Rita jail without incident. The vehicle was left parked at the location of arrest. It was Piedmont’s first transport to jail of arrested individuals in weeks. Many suspects have been arrested and cited but have not gone to jail because of COVID-19 limitations on jail capacity.
